Can you explain Article 133 of the Philippine Civil Code about donations between spouses?

Article 133 states that any donation between spouses made during the marriage is void. This means that spouses cannot give each other property or assets while they are both alive. However, there are two exceptions: first, if the donation is to take effect after the death of the donor (such as a gift made in a will), it is allowed. Second, moderate gifts given by one spouse to the other on occasions of family rejoicing, like birthdays, anniversaries, or holidays, are also allowed. The purpose is to prevent undue influence between spouses and protect family assets.

Paki-paliwanag ang Artikulo 1276 ng Civil Code ng Pilipinas tungkol sa merger o confusion of rights.

Ayon sa Artikulo 1276, kapag ang katangian ng pinagkakautangan at may utang ay napagsama sa iisang tao (merger o confusion) sa kaso ng pangunahing may utang o pinagkakautangan, ang obligasyon ay napapawi, at ito ay nakikinabang sa mga guarantor o tagapanagot. Ibig sabihin, sila ay napapalaya sa kanilang pananagutan bilang guarantor. Ngunit kung ang merger o confusion ay nangyari sa katauhan ng isang guarantor, hindi napapawi ang pangunahing obligasyon; nananatili pa rin ang pananagutan ng pangunahing may utang.

### Question
A neighbor has been using a portion of my land for years with my permission, and now they claim they own it. They say I am estopped from denying their ownership because I allowed them to use it. Does Article 1433 apply here?

### Retrieved Context
---
**[1] RA386-ART1433**
Path: BOOK IV - OBLIGATIONS AND CONTRACTS > TITLE IV.—ESTOPPEL (n) > Art. 1433
Text: Estoppel may be in pais or by deed.
Source: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocsfriendly/2/53360
---

Under Article 1433, estoppel may be in pais or by deed. Estoppel in pais arises from a person's conduct or representation that leads another to believe in a certain state of facts, and that other person relies on it to their detriment. In your situation, merely allowing someone to use your land does not automatically create estoppel; there must be a representation that you will not assert ownership, and the other party must have relied on that to their detriment. If such elements are proven, estoppel in pais may apply, preventing you from denying their claim of ownership. Estoppel by deed, on the other hand, arises from a written instrument, such as a deed of sale or acknowledgment, where a party is precluded from denying the truth of the statements contained therein. Thus, Article 1433 recognizes these two modes of estoppel.

---

- RA386-ART1433 — Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines): https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocsfriendly/2/53360

Paki-paliwanag po ang Artikulo 493 ng Civil Code tungkol sa co-ownership.

Ayon sa Artikulo 493, ang bawat co-owner ay may ganap na pagmamay-ari sa kanyang bahagi at sa mga bunga at benepisyo nito. Maaari niya itong ibenta, isangla, italaga, o ipagamit sa iba, maliban kung may personal na karapatan na kasangkot. Ngunit ang epekto ng pagbebenta o pagsasangla ay limitado lamang sa bahaging mapupunta sa kanya kapag hinati na ang co-ownership.

Sinasabi ng Artikulo 611 na kung ang isang usufruct ay itinatag para sa dalawa o higit pang mga tao na buhay noong panahong itinatag ito, hindi ito matatapos kapag namatay ang isa sa kanila. Pwede mo bang ipaliwanag ang Artikulo 1181 ng Civil Code ng Pilipinas tungkol sa conditional obligations?

Ayon sa Artikulo 1181, sa mga obligasyong may kondisyon, ang pagkakaroon ng mga karapatan, gayundin ang pagkawala o pagkapawi ng mga karapatang nakuha na, ay nakasalalay sa pangyayari ng kondisyon. Ibig sabihin, kung suspensive ang kondisyon, makakamit mo lamang ang karapatan kapag nangyari ang kondisyon. Kung resolutory naman, mawawala o mapapawi ang mga karapatan mo kapag nangyari ang kondisyon. Ang pangyayari ng kondisyon ang siyang nagbibigay-bisa sa mga epekto sa mga karapatan.

### Question
My father, a German citizen, lived in the Philippines for many years and died last month. He owned a house and lot in Quezon City, a bank account in Manila, and also an apartment in Berlin. His siblings in Germany claim that under German law they are entitled to a bigger share, while my mother says Philippine law should apply because the properties are in the Philippines. Could you explain which law governs the distribution of his estate?

### Retrieved Context
---
**[1] RA386-ART16**
Path: PRELIMINARY TITLE > CH 1 - EFFECT AND APPLICATION OF LAWS > Art. 16
Text: Real property as well as personal property is subject to the law of the country where it is situated.
However, intestate and testamentary successions, both with respect to the order of succession and to the amount of successional rights and to the intrinsic validity of testamentary provisions, shall be regulated by the national law of the person whose succession is under consideration, whatever may be the nature of the property and regardless of the country wherein said property may be found.
Source: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocsfriendly/2/53360
---

Under Article 16 of the Philippine Civil Code, property is generally subject to the law of the country where it is situated. However, there is a specific exception for succession. Intestate and testamentary successions, including the order of succession, the amount of successional rights, and the intrinsic validity of testamentary provisions, are regulated by the national law of the person whose succession is under consideration, regardless of the nature and location of the property. Since your father was a German citizen, German national law will govern the distribution of his estate, even for the properties located in the Philippines. This means that the shares of the heirs, who inherits, and the validity of any will provisions must be determined according to German law, not Philippine law, despite the properties being in Quezon City and Manila. Therefore, your father's siblings' claim that German law applies is correct in principle, and your mother's argument that Philippine law should apply because the properties are in the Philippines is not supported by Article 16.

---

**📚 Sources:**
- RA386-ART16 — Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines): https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocsfriendly/2/53360

Can you explain Article 421 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 421 of the Philippine Civil Code provides that all property of the State which is not of the character stated in the preceding article (Article 420, which enumerates property of public dominion) is patrimonial property. Patrimonial property refers to property owned by the State in its private or proprietary capacity, which may be alienated or disposed of, unlike property of public dominion which is intended for public use or public service and is generally inalienable.

Can you explain Article 676 of the Philippine Civil Code in simple terms?

Article 676 provides a legal easement for drainage. If a house has a yard or court that is completely enclosed by other houses, and there is no way to drain rainwater through the house itself, the owner can demand that an easement of drainage be established over neighboring land. The water must be given an outlet at the point of the adjacent properties where it can flow out most easily, and a conduit must be constructed in a way that causes the least damage to the servient estate (the property being used). The owner must also pay proper compensation (indemnity) for the use or damage.

### Question
I have been occupying a piece of land for 20 years without the owner's permission. Can I claim ownership through prescription? Also, my neighbor owes me money from 15 years ago, but I never demanded payment. Can I still collect? Please explain using Article 1106.

### Retrieved Context
---
**[1] RA386-ART1106**
Path: BOOK III - DIFFERENT MODES OF ACQUIRING OWNERSHIP > TITLE V.—PRESCRIPTION > CH 1 - GENERAL PROVISIONS > Art. 1106
Text: By prescription, one acquires ownership and other real rights through the lapse of time in the manner and under the conditions laid down by law.
In the same way, rights and actions are lost by prescription.
Source: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocsfriendly/2/53360
---

Under Article 1106 of the Civil Code, you may acquire ownership of the land through prescription if your possession meets the legal requirements. For acquisitive prescription of real property, the law generally requires possession that is in the concept of an owner, public, peaceful, uninterrupted, and for the period prescribed by law. Depending on whether you have just title and good faith, the period may be 10 years (ordinary acquisitive prescription) or 30 years (extraordinary acquisitive prescription). If you have possessed the land openly, continuously, and adversely for 20 years, you may qualify under extraordinary prescription if no just title or good faith is present, provided all other conditions are met. However, mere occupation without these elements will not ripen into ownership. Regarding the debt, Article 1106 also provides that rights and actions are lost by prescription. Actions to collect a debt prescribe after a certain period set by law (e.g., 10 years for written contracts, 6 years for oral contracts). Since 15 years have passed without any demand or acknowledgment, the action to collect is likely barred by extinctive prescription. Therefore, you probably can no longer enforce the debt unless there was an interruption of prescription (such as a written acknowledgment or partial payment) that restarted the period.

---

**📚 Sources:**
- RA386-ART1106 — Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines): https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocsfriendly/2/53360

### Question
I sold a piece of land to a buyer. We verbally agreed on a price of 500,000 pesos. However, when the buyer prepared the written contract, he changed the price to 50,000 pesos without my knowledge. I signed the contract thinking it stated 500,000 pesos. Now the buyer insists the contract says 50,000 pesos. What can I do under Philippine law?

### Retrieved Context
---
**[1] RA386-ART1362**
Path: BOOK IV - OBLIGATIONS AND CONTRACTS > TITLE II.—CONTRACTS > CH 4 > Art. 1362
Text: If one party was mistaken and the other acted fraudulently or inequitably in such a way that the instrument does not show their true intention, the former may ask for the reformation of the instrument.
Source: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocsfriendly/2/53360
---

Under Article 1362 of the Philippine Civil Code, if one party was mistaken about the terms of the contract and the other party acted fraudulently or inequitably in such a way that the written instrument does not show their true intention, the mistaken party may ask for the reformation of the instrument. In your situation, you were mistaken about the price stated in the written contract because you believed it reflected the agreed 500,000 pesos, while the buyer fraudulently changed it to 50,000 pesos. This fraudulent act caused the document to not reflect your true intention. Therefore, you may file a case for reformation of the contract, asking the court to correct the written instrument to reflect the true agreed price of 500,000 pesos.

---

- RA386-ART1362 — Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines): https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocsfriendly/2/53360

Can you explain Article 1065 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 1065 states that parents are not obligated to include in the collation of their parents' (ascendants') inheritance any property that was donated by the ascendants to the parents' children (i.e., the grandchildren of the donors). In other words, if a grandparent gives a gift to a grandchild, and later the grandparent dies, the child (parent of the grandchild) does not have to account for that gift when computing their share of the grandparent's estate. This is an exception to the general rule on collation, which requires heirs to bring back donations they received from the decedent so that the estate can be divided equally among compulsory heirs. This article protects donations given directly to grandchildren from being collated by their parents.

### Question
I have been possessing and cultivating a piece of agricultural land for over 20 years, treating it as my own. Now, a person came forward claiming to be the owner and is demanding that I show my title or prove my right to possess. I don't have a formal title, but I have been in continuous possession. Do I have to prove my title? What does the law say about my situation?

### Retrieved Context
---
**[1] RA386-ART541**
Path: BOOK II - PROPERTY, OWNERSHIP, AND ITS MODIFICATIONS > TITLE V.—POSSESSION > CH 3 - EFFECTS OF POSSESSION > Art. 541
Text: A possessor in the concept of owner has in his favor the legal presumption that he possesses with a just title and he cannot be obliged to show or prove it.
Source: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocsfriendly/2/53360
---

Under Article 541 of the Civil Code, since you possess the land in the concept of owner (treating it as your own), you enjoy a legal presumption that you possess with a just title. This means you cannot be obliged to show or prove your title. The burden of proof shifts to the person claiming ownership to present evidence that rebuts your presumed just title. However, note that this is a presumption of just title in your favor regarding possession, not a conclusive proof of ownership. The claimant may still present evidence to overcome the presumption. Therefore, you are not required to prove your title initially; instead, the other party must disprove your presumed valid possession.

---

- RA386-ART541 — Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines): https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocsfriendly/2/53360

Paki-paliwanag po ang Artikulo 1153 ng Civil Code tungkol sa prescription ng mga aksyon para humingi ng accounting.

Ipinapaliwanag ng Artikulo 1153 ang simula ng panahon ng prescription para sa dalawang uri ng aksyon. Una, ang aksyon upang humingi ng accounting ay nagsisimula ang prescription mula sa araw na tumigil sa kanilang mga tungkulin ang mga taong dapat mag-render ng accounting. Pangalawa, ang aksyon na nagmumula sa resulta ng accounting ay nagsisimula lamang ang prescription mula sa petsa kung kailan kinilala ang resulta sa pamamagitan ng kasunduan ng mga interesadong partido.

### Question
My husband took out a loan from a lending company without my knowledge or consent. He said he used the money to pay off his personal gambling debts. Now the lending company is threatening to seize our conjugal property, including our family car and savings. Can they do that? The loan did not benefit our family in any way.

### Retrieved Context
---
**[1] RA386-ART204**
Path: BOOK I - PERSONS > TITLE VI.—PROPERTY RELATIONS BETWEEN - HUSBAND AND WIFE > CH 6 > Art. 204
Text: Debts contracted by either spouse without the consent of the other shall be chargeable against the community to the extent that the family may have been benefited thereby.
Source: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocsfriendly/2/53360
---

Under Article 204 of the Civil Code, a debt contracted by one spouse without the consent of the other can only be charged against the community property to the extent that the family benefited from it. Here, your husband contracted the loan without your consent and used the proceeds to pay his personal gambling debts. This use provided no benefit to the family. Therefore, the community property (your conjugal assets such as the family car and savings) cannot be held liable for this debt. The lending company can only pursue your husband's separate property, not the common funds or property of the marriage. You are not personally liable, and the community is not obligated to pay. You may inform the creditor of this legal limitation.

---

**📚 Sources:**
- RA386-ART204 — Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines): https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocsfriendly/2/53360

Paki-paliwanag po ang Artikulo 1319 ng Civil Code ng Pilipinas.

Ayon sa Artikulo 1319, ang pagsang-ayon (consent) ay nabubuo sa pagkakatagpo ng alok (offer) at pagtanggap (acceptance) hinggil sa bagay at dahilan ng kontrata. Dapat tiyak ang alok at walang pasubali ang pagtanggap. Kung ang pagtanggap ay may pagbabago sa mga termino, ito ay itinuturing na bagong alok o counter-offer. Kapag ang pagtanggap ay ipinadala sa pamamagitan ng sulat o telegrama, ang nag-alok ay hindi pa mananagot hangga't hindi niya nalalaman ang pagtanggap. Sa ganitong kaso, ang kontrata ay ipinapalagay na ginawa sa lugar kung saan ginawa ang alok.

### Question
I purchased a cow from a local trader 30 days ago. A week after the purchase, I found out that the cow has a contagious disease that makes it unfit for breeding. I want to return the cow and get a refund, or at least get a price reduction. Can I still do that? What does the law say about my rights?

### Retrieved Context
---
**[1] RA386-ART1580**
Path: BOOK IV - OBLIGATIONS AND CONTRACTS > TITLE VI.—SALES > CH 4 - OBLIGATIONS OF THE VENDOR > SEC 3.—Conditions and Warranties > Art. 1580
Text: In the sale of animals with redhibitory defects, the vendee shall also enjoy the right mentioned in article 1567; but he must make use thereof within the same period which has been fixed for the exercise of the redhibitory action.
Source: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocsfriendly/2/53360
---

Under Article 1580 of the Civil Code, when an animal is sold with redhibitory defects, the buyer has the right under Article 1567 to either rescind the sale (return the animal and get a refund) or demand a proportional reduction of the price. However, this right must be exercised within the same period fixed for the redhibitory action, which is 40 days from the delivery of the animal. In your case, you bought the cow 30 days ago and discovered the disease a week later. Since only 30 days have passed, you are still within the 40-day period to bring the redhibitory action or demand a price reduction. You must act promptly before the 40 days expire. The contagious disease that makes the cow unfit for breeding likely qualifies as a redhibitory defect under the law, provided it existed at the time of sale and was hidden. Therefore, you still have time to either return the cow for a full refund or ask for a price reduction, but you need to take action immediately.

---

- RA386-ART1580 — Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines): https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocsfriendly/2/53360

### Question
My wife owns a commercial building she inherited from her parents. The monthly rental income from that building goes to our conjugal partnership. Lately, our family's daily expenses have increased, and the conjugal funds are not enough. Can we use the building itself to cover our daily needs?

### Retrieved Context
---
**[1] RA386-ART138**
Path: BOOK I - PERSONS > TITLE VI.—PROPERTY RELATIONS BETWEEN - HUSBAND AND WIFE > CH 3 - PARAPHERNAL PROPERTY > Art. 138
Text: The fruits of the paraphernal property form part of the assets of the conjugal partnership, and shall be subject to the payment of the expenses of the marriage.
The property itself shall also be subject to the daily expenses of the family, if the property of the conjugal partnership and the husband's capital are not sufficient therefor.
Source: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocsfriendly/2/53360
---

Under Article 138, the rental income from your wife's paraphernal property (the building) already forms part of the conjugal partnership assets. That income is subject to the payment of marriage expenses. Since the conjugal partnership assets, including that rental income, and your own capital as the husband are insufficient for the daily expenses of the family, the paraphernal property itself—the building—may be used to cover those daily expenses. This means the building can be utilized or even disposed of to meet the family's daily needs, as long as the insufficiency of conjugal funds is established.

---

**📚 Sources:**
- RA386-ART138 — Republic Act No. 386 (Civil Code of the Philippines): https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocsfriendly/2/53360

### Question
I am a 25-year-old woman. My fiancé and I want to get married at our family home because my father is bedridden and cannot go to the church or city hall. Is it legal for us to have our wedding ceremony at home under Philippine law?

### Retrieved Context
---
**[1] RA386-ART57**

The second-hand car is classified as movable or personal property because it can be moved from place to place without changing its essence. This basic classification determines the legal rules that will apply to your ownership, transfer, and registration of these properties. For more specific details, you would need to refer to the subsequent articles of the Civil Code that enumerate what are considered immovable and movable, but Article 414 establishes the fundamental dichotomy.

Kaya, ang pagsingil ng supplier para sa danyos ay maaaring tama kung may aktwal na pagkalugi, ngunit ang buong natitirang bayad ay hindi awtomatikong dapat bayaran kung ang muling pagbebenta ay nakabawi na ng halaga ng mga prutas.

### Question
I am a neighbor of a property. I noticed that my neighbor entered into a contract with someone to use his house as a gambling den, which is illegal. Can I file a case to declare that contract void because it is illegal? I am not a party to the contract, and I am not directly affected by it. **[1] RA386-ART1421**
Path: BOOK IV - OBLIGATIONS AND CONTRACTS > TITLE II.—CONTRACTS > CH 9 - VOID OR INEXISTENT CONTRACTS[1] > Art. 1421
Text: The defense of illegality of contract is not available to third persons whose interests are not directly affected.
Source: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocsfriendly/2/53360
---

Under Article 1421 of the Civil Code, the defense of illegality of a contract cannot be invoked by third persons whose interests are not directly affected. In your situation, as a neighbor, you are a third person to the contract between your neighbor and the other party. Unless you can show that the illegal contract directly affects your own interests (for example, causing you direct harm or injury), you cannot file a case to declare the contract void solely on the ground of its illegality. The law restricts this defense to the parties to the contract or to those who have a direct legal interest in it. While you may report the illegal activity to the appropriate authorities for them to take action, you cannot personally challenge the contract's validity on the ground of illegality if you are not directly affected by the contract itself.

### Question
I bought a blank canvas and gave it to my friend who is a painter. She painted a beautiful portrait on it. Now we have a disagreement: she says she owns the painting because under Article 468, the canvas is just an accessory. I think since I bought the canvas, I should own the painting. Who is right under the law?

### Retrieved Context
---
**[1] RA386-ART468**
Path: BOOK II - PROPERTY, OWNERSHIP, AND ITS MODIFICATIONS > TITLE II.—OWNERSHIP > CH 2 - RIGHT OF ACCESSION > SEC 3.—Right of Accession with Respect to Movable Property > Art. 468
Text: If it cannot be determined by the rule given in the preceding article which of the two things incorporated is the principal one, the thing of the greater value shall be so considered, and as between two things of equal value, that of the greater volume.
In painting and sculpture, writings, printed matter, engraving and lithographs, the board, metal, stone, canvas, paper or parchment shall be deemed the accessory thing.
Source: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocsfriendly/2/53360
---

Under Article 468 of the Civil Code, when two movable things are incorporated and it cannot be determined which is principal under Article 467, the thing of greater value is principal, or if equal value, the one of greater volume. More importantly, Article 468 expressly provides that in painting, sculpture, writings, printed matter, engraving, and lithographs, the board, metal, stone, canvas, paper, or parchment shall be deemed the accessory thing. This means that in a painting, the canvas (the material) is accessory, and the painting itself (the artistic work) is the principal thing. Applying this to your situation: your friend painted a portrait on your canvas. The canvas is clearly accessory, while the painting (the creative work) is principal. Therefore, the painting as a whole is considered the principal object. Ownership of the principal thing generally determines ownership of the whole, subject to rules on accession and indemnity. If your friend acted in good faith—meaning she did not know the canvas belonged to you or had no intent to deprive you of it—she would acquire ownership of the painting as the principal, but she must reimburse you for the value of the canvas. Conversely, if she acted in bad faith, she may lose the painting or be obliged to pay damages. Thus, under Article 468, your friend has a strong basis to claim the painting as the principal, but she must pay you for the canvas if she was in good faith.

### Question
I have a situation: My friend borrowed ₱50,000 from me, and separately, I owe him ₱30,000 for some equipment I bought. Both debts are already due, and there's no dispute about the amounts. I want to just pay him the difference of ₱20,000 and consider the rest compensated. Is that allowed under Philippine law?

### Retrieved Context
---
**[1] RA386-ART1279**
Path: BOOK IV - OBLIGATIONS AND CONTRACTS > TITLE I.—OBLIGATIONS > CH 4 - EXTINGUISHMENT OF OBLIGATIONS > SEC 5.—Compensation > Art. 1279
Text: In order that compensation may be proper, it is necessary:
(1) That each one of the obligors be bound principally, and that he be at the same time a principal creditor of the other;
(2) That both debts consist in a sum of money, or if the things due are consumable, they be of the same kind, and also of the same quality if the latter has been stated;
(3) That the two debts be due;
(4) That they be liquidated and demandable;
(5) That over neither of them there be any retention or controversy, commenced by third persons and communicated in due time to the debtor.
Source: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocsfriendly/2/53360
---

Under Article 1279 of the Civil Code, compensation can properly take place if all the requisites are present. In your scenario, both debts are monetary, both are due, and they appear liquidated and demandable, with no third-party claims. You and your friend are each principal debtor and creditor of the other. Therefore, compensation may operate, and you can validly pay only the difference of ₱20,000, extinguishing both debts to the extent of ₱30,000. However, if any of the listed conditions fails (e.g., one debt is not yet due, or there is a pending controversy communicated by a third person), compensation cannot occur, and you would have to pay the full amount while separately demanding payment from your friend.

Can you explain Article 874 of the Philippine Civil Code about conditions in wills that prohibit marriage?

Article 874 of the Philippine Civil Code provides that a condition in a will that absolutely prohibits someone from marrying (whether it is a first marriage or a subsequent marriage) is considered void and as if it was never written. This means the inheritance or devise will be given to the beneficiary without that condition. However, there is an exception: such a condition is valid if it is imposed on a widow or widower by the deceased spouse, or by that deceased spouse's ascendants or descendants. This allows a spouse to leave property to the surviving spouse on condition that they do not remarry. Furthermore, even if an absolute condition against marriage is void, the testator may still validly give someone a right of usufruct, an allowance, or some personal prestation (like a regular payment) for as long as that person remains unmarried or in widowhood. So restrictions tied to benefits while unmarried are allowed, but outright prohibitions on marriage as a condition for inheritance are generally not enforceable except for the specific case of widows/widowers.

Therefore, the primary basis for your claim is the penal law, but the Civil Code supplements it, allowing you to pursue remedies under quasi-delict if you choose.

I never had a title, but I treated the land as my own, built a house, and fenced it. Recently, a distant relative surfaced with an old deed claiming he is the registered owner and demanding I vacate. Under Article 525 of the Civil Code, was my possession in the concept of owner or merely as a holder? How does this affect my claim of ownership through prescription?

### Retrieved Context

**[1] RA386-ART525**
Path: BOOK II - PROPERTY, OWNERSHIP, AND ITS MODIFICATIONS > TITLE V.—POSSESSION > CH 1 - POSSESSION AND THE KINDS THEREOF > Art. 525
Text: The possession of things or rights may be had in one of two concepts: either in the concept of owner, or in that of the holder of the thing or right to keep or enjoy it, the ownership pertaining to another person.
Source: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocsfriendly/2/53360
---

Article 525 of the Civil Code provides that possession may be had either in the concept of owner or in the concept of a holder who keeps or enjoys the thing while ownership belongs to another. Possession in the concept of owner exists when a person possesses a thing as his own, believing himself to be the owner and performing acts of ownership, even without a title. In your case, you have occupied and farmed the land for over 20 years, paid real property taxes, built a house, and fenced the property, all while believing it was yours due to your father's verbal conveyance. These are clear acts of dominion indicating possession in the concept of owner, not merely as a holder who recognizes another's ownership. This classification is significant because possession in the concept of owner, if it is public, peaceful, and uninterrupted for the period required by law, can ripen into ownership through ordinary or extraordinary acquisitive prescription. Since you possessed the land openly and continuously as an owner, your possession supports a claim of ownership by prescription, provided you meet the other statutory requirements (such as good faith, just title, and the applicable prescriptive period). In contrast, possession in the concept of a holder, such as that of a tenant or borrower, generally does not lead to ownership by prescription unless the holder repudiates the owner's title and converts the possession into one in the concept of owner. Therefore, based on your description, your possession was in the concept of owner, which strengthens your potential claim to the land through acquisitive prescription. You should consult a lawyer to evaluate the specific facts, the nature of your father's conveyance, and the exact period of possession to determine whether you have acquired ownership under the law.

### Question
I bought a parcel of land from a person I believed was the owner. I have been in possession of the land for many years, paying taxes and making improvements. Later, I discovered that the seller was not the true owner because the title had a defect. I want to know if I can still acquire the land through prescription and how good faith affects my claim. Can you advise me?

### Retrieved Context

**[1] RA386-ART1128**
Path: BOOK III - DIFFERENT MODES OF ACQUIRING OWNERSHIP > TITLE V.—PRESCRIPTION > CH 2 - PRESCRIPTION OF OWNERSHIP AND OTHER REAL RIGHTS > Art. 1128
Text: The conditions of good faith required for possession in articles 526, 527, 528, and 529 of this Code are likewise necessary for the determination of good faith in the prescription of ownership and other real rights.
Source: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocsfriendly/2/53360

Under Article 1128 of the Civil Code, the good faith required for prescription of ownership is the same as that required for possession under Articles 526 to 529. Good faith consists in the possessor's belief that the person from whom they received the thing was the owner and could transmit ownership, and that they were unaware of any flaw in their title or mode of acquisition. In your case, you initially believed the seller was the true owner, so you possessed the land in good faith. However, good faith ceases from the moment you became aware of the defect in the title. For ordinary prescription, which requires good faith and just title, the period of possession must be computed only during the time you were in good faith. Once you learned of the defect, the character of your possession changes from good faith to bad faith. Therefore, you may still acquire the land through extraordinary prescription, which does not require good faith, but requires a longer period of possession (30 years for immovables under the Civil Code). The time during which you possessed in good faith may be counted, but the period of bad faith possession cannot be credited towards ordinary prescription. To succeed in acquiring ownership, you must meet the required period of possession under the applicable type of prescription.

Can you explain Article 852 of the Philippine Civil Code? What does it mean when the shares of instituted heirs don't add up to the whole estate?

Article 852 addresses a situation in a will where the testator names several heirs and gives each a specific fractional share (aliquot part) of the estate, but the sum of these shares is less than the whole estate or the whole free portion. Nevertheless, an agreement to keep the thing undivided for a certain period of time, not exceeding ten years, shall be valid. This term may be extended by a new agreement.

---

Under Article 494 of the Civil Code, you, as a co-owner, have the right to demand partition of the property at any time. The general rule is that no co-owner can be compelled to remain in co-ownership. However, the law allows an agreement among co-owners to keep the property undivided for a certain period, but such period cannot exceed ten years. Any agreement exceeding ten years is void to the extent of the excess. In your case, the alleged 15-year agreement is invalid because it exceeds the maximum allowed by law. Therefore, you are not bound by it and can still demand partition. Additionally, the rule on prescription does not bar your right because as long as the co-ownership is recognized, prescription does not run against a co-owner. Unless there is a prohibition by a donor/testator (which is not mentioned) or a legal prohibition (e.g., property is not subject to partition due to its nature), you may proceed to demand partition of your share.

Can you explain Article 1596 of the Philippine Civil Code about the seller's action for damages when the buyer refuses to accept and pay for goods?

Article 1596 of the Philippine Civil Code deals with the situation where a buyer wrongfully neglects or refuses to accept and pay for the goods. In such case, the seller may file an action for damages for non-acceptance. The measure of damages is the estimated loss directly and naturally resulting from the buyer's breach of contract. The profit the seller would have made if the contract had been fully performed is also considered in awarding damages.

My father donated a parcel of land to my sister, but later he wanted to revoke the donation because she refused to support him in his old age. Unfortunately, my father died before he could file a case in court. Now I want to continue his fight and file the revocation case as his heir. Path: BOOK III - DIFFERENT MODES OF ACQUIRING OWNERSHIP > TITLE III.—DONATION > CH 4 - REVOCATION AND REDUCTION OF DONATIONS > Art. 770

Under Article 770 of the Civil Code, the action for revocation of a donation is personal to the donor and does not transmit to his heirs if he did not file the complaint during his lifetime. Since your father did not institute the revocation case before his death, you, as his heir, cannot file it, even if he could have done so and even if he died within one year from the time he could have filed. Furthermore, the action cannot be brought against the heirs of the donee unless a complaint was already filed against the donee before her death. Since no complaint was filed against your sister while she was alive, you cannot file the case against her children. Therefore, under this article, you have no legal standing to pursue the revocation.

### Question
My father wrote in his will that he is disinheriting me because I married someone he did not approve of. I am his legitimate child and I believe I am a compulsory heir. Is this disinheritance valid?

Under Article 915, a compulsory heir may only be deprived of his legitime through disinheritance if the cause is one of those expressly stated by law. The law provides specific grounds for disinheritance, such as when the heir has been convicted of an attempt against the life of the testator, or has accused the testator of a crime punishable by imprisonment of six years or more, if the accusation is found to be false, among others. Marrying against the testator's wishes, in itself, is not a ground for disinheritance under the Civil Code unless it falls under a specific provision (e.g., if the heir contracted marriage despite the testator's opposition under certain age conditions, but even then the requirements are strict). In this scenario, the father's reason is purely based on personal disapproval of the marriage, which is not a cause expressly stated by law. Therefore, the disinheritance would not be valid, and the compulsory heir retains the right to his legitime.

Can you explain what Article 960 of the Philippine Civil Code says about when legal or intestate succession takes place?

Article 960 states that legal succession (also called intestate succession) applies when: (1) a person dies without a will, or with a void will, or one that lost its validity; (2) the will does not institute an heir or does not dispose of all the property, so legal succession applies to the undisposed portion; (3) a suspensive condition for an heir's institution is not fulfilled, or the heir dies before the testator, or repudiates the inheritance, and there is no substitution and no right of accretion; or (4) the instituted heir is incapable of succeeding, except as provided in the Code. In these cases, the estate is distributed to the legal heirs according to the rules on intestate succession.

Can you explain Article 1299 of the Philippine Civil Code about novation and conditions?

Article 1299 states that if the original obligation had a suspensive or resolutory condition, the new obligation created through novation will be under the same condition, unless the parties agree otherwise. A suspensive condition is one that must happen before the obligation becomes effective, while a resolutory condition is one that extinguishes the obligation when it happens. So when an obligation is novated (changed or replaced by a new one), any condition attached to the old obligation is automatically carried over to the new obligation, unless the parties explicitly stipulate a different condition or none at all.

If you and your husband have a separation of property regime, you would instead contribute proportionately to the family expenses.

### Question
I have been occupying a parcel of land for 8 years. The previous occupant, who sold me his rights, had been there for 4 years. I want to claim ownership through acquisitive prescription which requires 10 years of uninterrupted possession. My question is: can I combine my 8 years with his 4 years? Also, if I started occupying on January 1, 2015, and the period should end on January 1, 2025, does that count as exactly 10 years? I'm confused about which days to count.

### Retrieved Context
---
**[1] RA386-ART1138**
Path: BOOK III - DIFFERENT MODES OF ACQUIRING OWNERSHIP > TITLE V.—PRESCRIPTION > CH 3 - PRESCRIPTION OF ACTIONS > Art. 1138
Text: In the computation of time necessary for prescription the following rules shall be observed:
(1) The present possessor may complete the period necessary for prescription by tacking his possession to that of his grantor or predecessor in interest;
(2) It is presumed that the present possessor who was also the possessor at a previous time, has continued to be in possession during the intervening time, unless there is proof to the contrary;
(3) The first day shall be excluded and the last day included.
Source: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocsfriendly/2/53360
---

Under Article 1138 of the Civil Code, the rules for computing prescription apply to your situation. First, you are allowed to tack your possession to that of your predecessor or grantor. This means you can add the 4 years of the previous occupant to your 8 years, giving you a total of 12 years, which exceeds the required 10-year period for acquisitive prescription. Second, the law presumes that if you were in possession at a previous time and are still in possession now, your possession is continuous, unless there is proof of interruption. Since you have been continuously occupying the land after acquiring it from the previous occupant, this presumption supports your claim. Third, regarding the counting of days: the first day of possession is excluded, and the last day is included. So if you started possessing on January 1, 2015, you do not count January 1 itself; the period starts on January 2, 2015. Ten years later, the period would be completed at the end of January 1, 2025 (the last day being included). Therefore, by January 1, 2025, you would have satisfied the 10-year requirement, provided there is no evidence of interruption. In summary, you may combine the periods, the continuity is presumed, and the day-counting works in your favor.

Article 499 states that when co-owners divide (partition) a property they own together, the division cannot harm the rights of third parties. In short, partition only affects the co-owners' shares among themselves; it does not wipe out the rights of outsiders.

One sibling refuses to pay his share of the real property taxes, saying he will just give up a portion of his share to cover it. But his share is already quite small, and giving up more would leave him with a tiny fraction that would make decision-making and future sale very difficult. Under Article 488 of the Civil Code, each co-owner has the right to compel the other co-owners to contribute to the expenses for preservation of the property and to taxes. A co-owner may exempt himself from this obligation by renouncing so much of his undivided interest as may be equivalent to his share of the expenses and taxes. However, such waiver cannot be made if it is prejudicial to the co-ownership. In your situation, if your sibling's renunciation of a portion of his undivided interest would result in an extremely small fractional share that undermines effective management, complicates decision-making, or diminishes the overall value or marketability of the property, then it may be considered prejudicial to the co-ownership. Therefore, he cannot unilaterally renounce his interest to avoid paying taxes if it would harm the common property. He remains liable for his proportionate share of the real property taxes, and you and your other sibling can legally demand that he contribute.

Under Article 849 of the Civil Code, when a testator institutes a person and his children, they are all deemed instituted simultaneously and not successively. Can you explain Article 1187 of the Civil Code about the retroactive effects of conditional obligations?

Article 1187 provides that in a conditional obligation to give, once the condition is fulfilled, its effects retroact to the day the obligation was constituted. For obligations to do or not to do, the courts decide the retroactive effect on a case-by-case basis.

### Question
My father died and left a will. He had three children: me, my brother, and my sister. In his will, he left the free portion equally to the three of us. My brother decided to repudiate his share. I want to know if his share will go to me and my sister by accretion. Also, what if my brother also repudiated his legitime? Who gets that?

### Retrieved Context
---
**[1] RA386-ART1021**
Path: BOOK III - DIFFERENT MODES OF ACQUIRING OWNERSHIP > TITLE IV.—SUCCESSION > CH 4 - PROVISIONS COMMON TO TESTATE AND INTESTATE SUCCESSIONS > SEC 1.—Right of Accretion > Art. 1021
Text: Among the compulsory heirs the right of accretion shall take place only when the free portion is left to two or more of them, or to any one of them and to a stranger.
Should the part repudiated be the legitime, the other co-heirs shall succeed to it in their own right, and not by the right of accretion.
Source: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocsfriendly/2/53360
---

Under Article 1021 of the Civil Code, among compulsory heirs, the right of accretion only applies to the free portion, not to the legitime. In your situation, if your father left the free portion equally to the three of you (all compulsory heirs), and your brother repudiates his share of the free portion, that repudiated share will be added to the shares of you and your sister by accretion, provided your father did not provide otherwise in the will. This means the free portion will be divided equally between you and your sister. However, if your brother also repudiates his legitime (the portion reserved by law for compulsory heirs), Article 1021 provides that the other compulsory heirs (you and your sister) will succeed to that legitime in their own right, not by accretion. This means the repudiated legitime will be distributed between you and your sister according to the rules on legitime, not as an added testamentary share. Since you are all children of the deceased, the legitime would normally be divided equally among all children, so if one repudiates, the remaining children take that share equally in their own right as compulsory heirs.

Can you explain Article 1498 of the Philippine Civil Code? What does it mean when sale is made through a public instrument, and how does delivery of movable property work with keys?

Article 1498 of the Philippine Civil Code deals with the delivery of the thing sold in a contract of sale. It states that when the sale is made through a public instrument (a notarized document), the execution of that instrument is considered equivalent to the delivery of the thing sold. This is a form of constructive delivery, meaning the buyer is deemed to have received the thing even without physical transfer, unless the deed itself states otherwise or it can be clearly inferred that the parties did not intend immediate delivery. For movable property, delivery can also be accomplished by delivering the keys to the place or depository where the movable is stored or kept. This is also a symbolic form of delivery. So, if you buy a car and sign a notarized deed of sale, the car is considered delivered upon signing, unless the deed says something different. If goods are stored in a warehouse, handing over the warehouse keys to the buyer constitutes delivery.

Can you explain what Article 1387 of the Civil Code says about contracts in fraud of creditors?

Article 1387 of the Philippine Civil Code provides legal presumptions of fraud when a debtor transfers property. First, if a debtor donates property (a gratuitous transfer) and does not reserve enough property to pay all debts he had before the donation, the donation is presumed to have been made in fraud of creditors. Second, if a debtor sells or otherwise transfers property by onerous title (for value) at a time when a judgment has been rendered against him or a writ of attachment has been issued against him, that transfer is also presumed fraudulent. The judgment or attachment does not need to refer to the specific property transferred, and it does not need to have been obtained by the person seeking to rescind the transfer. In addition to these presumptions, fraud against creditors may be proven by any other evidence allowed by law. These are disputable presumptions, so the opposing party may present evidence to overcome them.

Instead, it is disputably presumed that the payer intended to make a gift to the child. In your situation, since you paid for the lot but the title was placed in your daughter's name, the law presumes that you gave the property to her as a gift. This means that she is presumed to be the beneficial owner. To overcome this presumption and claim any rights over the property, you would need to present clear and convincing evidence that you did not intend to donate the property to your daughter, such as a written agreement or other proof of a contrary intention.

Can you explain Article 830 of the Philippine Civil Code about the revocation of wills?

Article 830 states that a will can only be revoked in three ways: (1) by implication of law, such as when a legal presumption automatically revokes it; (2) by executing a new will, codicil, or other writing that meets the formalities required for wills and revokes the previous will; or (3) by physically destroying the will—burning, tearing, cancelling, or obliterating it—with the intention of revoking it, done by the testator himself or by another person in the testator's presence and under his express direction. I have a mango farm that I allowed my neighbor to use as a usufructuary for five years. When the usufruct started, there were mango fruits already growing on the trees. Now that the usufruct is about to end, there are new mango fruits growing. Who owns the fruits in each situation, and do I need to reimburse my neighbor for his expenses?

### Retrieved Context
---
**[1] RA386-ART567**
Path: BOOK II - PROPERTY, OWNERSHIP, AND ITS MODIFICATIONS > TITLE VI.—USUFRUCT > CH 2 - RIGHTS OF THE USUFRUCTUARY > Art. 567
Text: Natural or industrial fruits growing at the time the usufruct begins, belong to the usufructuary.
Those growing at the time the usufruct terminates, belong to the owner.
In the preceding cases, the usufructuary, at the beginning of the usufruct, has no obligation to refund to the owner any expenses incurred; but the owner shall be obliged to reimburse at the termination of the usufruct, from the proceeds of the growing fruits, the ordinary expenses of cultivation, for seed, and other similar expenses incurred by the usufructuary.
The provisions of this article shall not prejudice the rights of third persons, acquired either at the beginning or at the termination of the usufruct.
Source: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocsfriendly/2/53360
---

Under Article 567 of the Civil Code, the mango fruits that were already growing at the time the usufruct began belong to your neighbor as the usufructuary. You, as the owner, are not entitled to any reimbursement from your neighbor for the fertilizer expenses you incurred before the usufruct started, because the usufructuary has no obligation to refund the owner for such prior expenses. The mango fruits that are still growing at the time the usufruct ends belong to you as the owner. However, you are obliged to reimburse your neighbor for the ordinary cultivation expenses, costs of seeds, and similar expenses he incurred during the usufruct, but only from the proceeds of the fruits that are still growing at the termination of the usufruct. If those proceeds are insufficient to cover all of his expenses, your obligation to reimburse is limited to the amount actually obtained from those growing fruits. This rule does not affect the rights of any third parties who may have acquired rights at the beginning or end of the usufruct.

Therefore, he cannot reclaim the strip of land based on the survey; he is bound by his earlier statement. This is a clear application of estoppel under Article 1431.

Until that announcement is made, the auctioneer may withdraw the goods from the sale unless the auction has been announced to be without reserve. However, once the hammer falls and the sale is announced, the contract is perfected and the seller can no longer withdraw the item. The seller's act of asking a friend to bid to increase the price violates this provision if no such notice was given. As a result, you may treat the sale as fraudulent and seek remedies such as rescission of the sale or damages.

Kalaunan, natuklasan ko na may malalaking bitak at problema sa pundasyon. Maaari ko bang kasuhan ng pandaraya ang engineer? Eksperto siya at umasa ako sa kanyang opinyon.

Path: BOOK IV - OBLIGATIONS AND CONTRACTS > TITLE II.—CONTRACTS > CH 2 - ESSENTIAL REQUISITES OF CONTRACTS > SEC 1.—Consent > Art. 1341
Text: A mere expression of an opinion does not signify fraud, unless made by an expert and the other party has relied on the former's special knowledge.

Sa ilalim ng Artikulo 1341 ng Civil Code, ang pagpapahayag lamang ng opinyon ay hindi pandaraya. Samakatuwid, kung mapapatunayan na ang opinyon ng engineer ay mali o mapanlinlang, at ikaw ay umasa dito sa iyong kapinsalaan, maaaring ituring itong pandaraya sa ilalim ng artikulong ito. Kung siya ay matapat na naniniwala na maayos ang bahay, maaaring ito ay kaso ng kapabayaan sa halip na pandaraya. Ngunit ang pagiging eksperto niya at ang iyong pag-asa sa kanya ay tumutugon sa mga kundisyon ng Artikulo 1341 para maisaalang-alang ang opinyon bilang posibleng pandaraya.

### Question
I ordered a custom-made wooden cabinet from a furniture maker in Pampanga. The seller shipped it via a trucking company he chose, but he didn't tell me which one or provide any tracking. The cabinet got badly damaged in transit. The seller claims that delivery to the trucking company counts as delivery to me, so I should bear the loss. But I think he should have arranged proper insurance and informed me. What does Article 1523 say about who bears the risk here?

### Retrieved Context
---
**[1] RA386-ART1523**
Path: BOOK IV - OBLIGATIONS AND CONTRACTS > TITLE VI.—SALES > CH 4 - OBLIGATIONS OF THE VENDOR > SEC 2.—Delivery of the Thing Sold > Art. 1523
Text: Where, in pursuance of a contract of sale, the seller is authorized or required to send the goods to the buyer, delivery of the goods to a carrier, whether named by the buyer or not, for the purpose of transmission to the buyer is deemed to be a delivery of the goods to the buyer, except in the cases provided for in article 1503, first, second and third paragraphs, or unless a contrary intent appears.
Unless otherwise authorized by the buyer, the seller must make such contract with the carrier on behalf of the buyer as may be reasonable, having regard to the nature of the goods and the other circumstances of the case. If the seller omit so to do, and the goods are lost or damaged in course of transit, the buyer may decline to treat the delivery to the carrier as a delivery to himself, or may hold the seller responsible in damages.
Unless otherwise agreed, where goods are sent by the seller to the buyer under circumstances in which the seller knows or ought to know that it is usual to insure, the seller must give such notice to the buyer as may enable him to insure them during their transit, and, if the seller fails to do so, the goods shall be deemed to be at his risk during such transit.
Source: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocsfriendly/2/53360
---

Under Article 1523 of the Civil Code, when a seller is required or authorized to send goods to the buyer, delivery to a carrier is generally deemed delivery to the buyer, which would shift the risk of loss to the buyer. However, this rule has important exceptions. First, the seller must make a reasonable contract with the carrier on behalf of the buyer, considering the nature of the goods and the circumstances. If the seller fails to do so and the goods are lost or damaged in transit, the buyer may decline to treat the delivery to the carrier as delivery to himself, or may hold the seller responsible for damages. In your case, if the seller did not select a competent carrier or did not arrange for appropriate handling for a custom-made wooden cabinet, that may be an unreasonable contract. Second, unless otherwise agreed, if goods are sent under circumstances where it is usual to insure, the seller must give notice to the buyer to enable the buyer to insure the goods during transit. If the seller fails to give such notice, the goods are at the seller's risk during transit. A custom-made wooden cabinet is valuable and fragile; it is usual to insure such goods. The seller did not inform you of the carrier or give you a chance to insure, so the risk remained with the seller during transit. Therefore, the loss falls on the seller, not on you. You may decline to accept the damaged cabinet as delivered to you and demand replacement or refund, or hold the seller liable for damages.

Can you explain Article 740 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding donations?

Article 740 provides that the same grounds of incapacity to inherit by will (testamentary succession) also apply to donations inter vivos (donations made during the lifetime of the donor). The law aims to prevent circumvention of prohibitions on who may inherit.

### Question
My siblings and I inherited our parents' house and lot. We agreed that I will pay them for their shares and they will transfer their rights to me. We executed a Deed of Sale. Later, one sibling claims it was not a partition but a sale, and now wants to question the valuation and avoid the partition rules. Is our transaction considered a partition under Article 1082?

### Retrieved Context
---
**[1] RA386-ART1082**
Path: BOOK III - DIFFERENT MODES OF ACQUIRING OWNERSHIP > TITLE IV.—SUCCESSION > CH 4 - PROVISIONS COMMON TO TESTATE AND INTESTATE SUCCESSIONS > SEC 6.—Partition and Distribution of the Estate > Art. 1082
Text: Every act which is intended to put an end to indivision among co-heirs and legatees or devisees is deemed to be a partition, although it should purport to be a sale, an exchange, a compromise, or any other transaction.
Source: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocsfriendly/2/53360
---

Under Article 1082, if the Deed of Sale was intended to end the co-ownership among co-heirs and effectively distribute the property to you, it is deemed a partition, even if labeled as a sale. The court will look beyond the form and consider the intent: the siblings agreed to terminate their indivision, you acquired their shares, and the co-ownership ended. Therefore, the transaction is legally a partition, subject to partition rules, including the right to rescind for lesion if the share received is less than one-fourth of the fair value under relevant provisions. Your sibling cannot escape the consequences of partition by labeling it a sale; the law treats it as partition to ensure the protection of co-heirs.

### Question
I am a farmer. Last year, the river near my property changed its course naturally. My one-hectare farmland was submerged by the new river path, and I lost that land completely. The old river bed is now dry and lies next to my neighbor's property. Who legally owns that old river bed now? Can I claim it, or can my neighbor buy it from me? How is the price determined?

### Retrieved Context
---
**[1] RA386-ART461**
Path: BOOK II - PROPERTY, OWNERSHIP, AND ITS MODIFICATIONS > TITLE II.—OWNERSHIP > CH 2 - RIGHT OF ACCESSION > SEC 2.—Right of Accession with Respect to > Art. 461
Text: River beds which are abandoned through the natural change in the course of the waters ipso facto belong to the owners whose lands are occupied by the new course in proportion to the area lost. However, the owners of the lands adjoining the old bed shall have the right to acquire the same by paying the value thereof, which value shall not exceed the value of the area occupied by the new bed.
Source: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocsfriendly/2/53360
---

Under Article 461 of the Civil Code, when a river abandons its old bed due to a natural change in its course, the abandoned river bed automatically belongs to the owners whose lands are occupied by the new course, in proportion to the area they lost. In your case, you lost one hectare of farmland to the new river course. Therefore, you are entitled to a portion of the abandoned old bed equal to the area you lost, i.e., one hectare, unless the old bed is smaller, in which case your share would be proportional. However, the owners of lands adjoining the old bed—your neighbor in this scenario—have the right to acquire that portion by paying its value. The value they must pay cannot exceed the value of the area occupied by the new course, which means the price cannot be more than the value of the one hectare you lost. So, you have a claim to that portion of the old bed, but your neighbor has the option to buy it from you at a price capped at the value of your lost land. If you and your neighbor cannot agree on the price, it may be determined by the court based on fair market value, but always with that maximum limit.

Article 162 states that if the husband alone donates or promises something to their common children for the purpose of securing their future or finishing their career, or if both spouses do so through a common agreement, the value of such donation or promise is charged to the conjugal partnership, unless they have stipulated that it should be satisfied from the separate property of one of them, in whole or in part. ### Question
I have been possessing a piece of land openly and continuously for 9 years, aiming to acquire it by extraordinary prescription which requires 30 years. However, last year a severe typhoon caused flooding that made the land inaccessible for 8 months. Does that interruption reset my 9 years of possession?

### Retrieved Context
---
**[1] RA386-ART1122**
Path: BOOK III - DIFFERENT MODES OF ACQUIRING OWNERSHIP > TITLE V.—PRESCRIPTION > CH 2 - PRESCRIPTION OF OWNERSHIP AND OTHER REAL RIGHTS > Art. 1122
Text: If the natural interruption is for only one year or less, the time elapsed shall be counted in favor of the prescription.
Source: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocsfriendly/2/53360
---

Under Article 1122 of the Civil Code, if a natural interruption lasts for only one year or less, the time elapsed before the interruption shall be counted in favor of the prescription. In your case, the flooding caused by the typhoon is a natural interruption, and it lasted for 8 months, which is less than one year. Therefore, the 9 years of possession you accumulated before the flooding are not lost; they continue to be counted. You may resume counting the prescriptive period from where it left off, so you still have 9 years credited toward the required 30 years.

Text: Every owner may increase the height of the party wall, doing so at his own expense and paying for any damage which may be caused by the work, even though such damage be temporary.

If the increased height or depth leads to higher expenses for preserving the party wall, he must pay an indemnity to cover those additional costs. Furthermore, if the existing party wall cannot bear the increased height, your neighbor is obliged to reconstruct the wall at his own expense. If the reconstruction requires making the wall thicker, he must provide the additional space from his own land, not from your property. Therefore, you are not liable for any of these expenses, damages, or additional maintenance costs.

My husband promised to give our son a piece of land to help him pursue his engineering degree. We did not specify whether this should come from our conjugal funds or from my husband's personal property. Now that we are having issues with our property relations, I want to know if this promise is a charge against the conjugal partnership or against my husband's separate assets. Since no agreement was made that the donation would be paid from your husband's personal property, the value of the land is a charge against the conjugal partnership. This means both of you, through the conjugal partnership, bear the obligation, not just your husband individually. The law presumes that such acts for the benefit of common children are for the family's benefit and thus a conjugal liability, unless the spouses expressly provide otherwise.

Pwede mo bang ipaliwanag ang Artikulo 599 ng Kodigo Sibil ng Pilipinas tungkol sa karapatan ng usufructuary na maningil ng mga matured credits?

Ang Artikulo 599 ng Kodigo Sibil ng Pilipinas ay tungkol sa karapatan ng isang usufructuary (taong may karapatang gamitin at pakinabangan ang ari-arian ng iba) na maningil ng mga matured credits na bahagi ng usufruct. Ang matured credit ay isang utang o obligasyong pinansyal na dapat nang bayaran. May dalawang sitwasyon ang batas:

1. Kung nakapagbigay ang usufructuary ng sapat na seguridad (bond o garantiya upang protektahan ang interes ng may-ari sa kapital), maaari niyang singilin ang mga matured credits at gamitin ang nakolektang pera sa anumang paraan na nais niya.

2. Kung hindi nakapagbigay ng seguridad ang usufructuary, o hindi sapat ang seguridad, hindi niya maaaring singilin ang mga credits nang walang pahintulot ng may-ari (ang taong may hawak ng hubad na titulo) o, kung tumanggi ang may-ari, ng korte. Kahit may pahintulot, kailangan niyang i-invest ang nakolektang kapital na may interes, ayon sa kasunduan sa may-ari o sa pahintulot ng korte, at kailangang may sapat na seguridad upang mapanatili ang buo ng kapital na napapailalim sa usufruct.

Sa madaling salita, pinoprotektahan ng batas ang karapatan ng may-ari sa kapital sa pamamagitan ng pag-aatas ng seguridad o pangangasiwa ng korte bago makuha ng usufructuary ang mga matured credits.

### Question
My wife inherited a receivable from her father that is payable in annual installments over 10 years. We are married under the conjugal partnership of gains. Some installments have been received during the marriage. How do we determine which portion of those installments belongs to her as her paraphernal property and which belongs to our conjugal partnership? Also, she has a life pension from an insurance policy that she acquired before our marriage. Are the monthly pension payments conjugal or her separate property?

### Retrieved Context
---
**[1] RA386-ART152**
Path: BOOK I - PERSONS > TITLE VI.—PROPERTY RELATIONS BETWEEN - HUSBAND AND WIFE > CH 4 - CONJUGAL PARTNERSHIP OF GAINS > SEC 3.—Conjugal Partnership Property > Art. 152
Text: If some credit payable in a certain number of years, or a life pension, should pertain to one of the spouses, the provisions of articles 156 and 157 shall be observed to determine what constitutes the paraphernal property and what forms the capital of the husband.
Source: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocsfriendly/2/53360
---

Under Article 152 of the Civil Code, we apply Articles 156 and 157 to your situation. For the credit payable in annual installments over 10 years: Under Article 156, the sums collected during the marriage are considered as the separate property (paraphernal property) of your wife, except the interest or income portion, which is conjugal partnership property. This means each installment must be broken down into its principal component (which returns the capital, i.e., the amount of the credit) and its interest component (which is the fruit of that capital). The principal portion becomes your wife's paraphernal property, while the interest portion belongs to the conjugal partnership. For the life pension: Under Article 157, the ownership of the life pension (the right to receive the pension) is considered as belonging to your wife, since she acquired it before marriage and it is her separate property. However, the payments or pensions received during the marriage are conjugal partnership property, because they are considered as fruits of her separate property. Therefore, the monthly pension payments are conjugal, but the right to the pension itself remains her paraphernal property. In summary: for the installment credit, split each installment into principal (paraphernal) and interest (conjugal); for the life pension, the entire periodic payment is conjugal, but the underlying right is paraphernal.

### Question
I have a spring that originates on my private land. The water flows through my property and then onto my neighbor's land. My neighbor claims that since the water flows across his property, he also has a right to use it. Is that correct? Who owns the spring water while it is on my land?

### Retrieved Context
---
**[1] RA386-ART503**
Path: BOOK II - PROPERTY, OWNERSHIP, AND ITS MODIFICATIONS > TITLE IV.—SOME SPECIAL PROPERTIES > CH 1 - WATERS > SEC 2.—The Use of Public Waters > Art. 503
Text: The following are of private ownership:
(1) Continuous or intermittent waters rising on lands of private ownership, while running through the same;
(2) Lakes and lagoons, and their beds, formed by Nature on such lands;
(3) Subterranean waters found on the same;
(4) Rain waters falling on said lands, as long as they remain within the boundaries;
(5) The beds of flowing waters, continuous or intermittent, formed by rain water, and those of brooks, crossing lands which are not of public dominion.
In every drain or aqueduct, the water, bed, banks and floodgates shall be considered as an integral part of the land or building for which the waters are intended. The owners of lands, through which or along the boundaries of which the aqueduct passes, cannot claim ownership over it, or any right to the use of its bed or banks, unless the claim is based on titles of ownership specifying the right or ownership claimed.
Source: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocsfriendly/2/53360
---

Under Article 503 of the Civil Code, continuous or intermittent waters rising on lands of private ownership, while running through the same, are of private ownership. This means that as long as the spring water is on your private land, you own it exclusively. Your neighbor cannot claim any ownership or right to use that water while it is within your property boundaries. The fact that the water later flows onto his land does not retroactively give him ownership over the portion still on your land. Once the water leaves your property and enters your neighbor's land, its legal status may change (for example, it may become part of a natural stream classified as public water under Article 502), but that does not affect your private ownership while it is on your land. Therefore, your neighbor's claim to use the water on your land is not supported by Article 503. Additionally, if there is any drain or aqueduct built to channel the water, that structure and its water, bed, banks, and floodgates are considered an integral part of the land for which the water is intended, and your neighbor cannot claim ownership over it unless he has a title specifying such right.

Can you explain Article 1108 of the Philippine Civil Code? What does it mean that prescription runs against certain persons?

Article 1108 states that prescription, both acquisitive and extinctive, runs against: (1) minors and incapacitated persons who have parents, guardians, or legal representatives; (2) absentees who have administrators, whether appointed by themselves before their disappearance or by courts; (3) persons living abroad who have managers or administrators; and (4) juridical persons, except the State and its subdivisions. This means that for these categories, time continues to run even though they may not personally manage their affairs, because they have representatives who are expected to act on their behalf. The article also provides that if a legal representative's negligence causes prescription to run, the person represented can claim damages from that representative.

My father’s will states that my brother will inherit our family land, but he must preserve it and then pass it to my son when my brother dies. My brother and my son were both alive when my father died. Is this allowed? Can my son later pass it to his own son as stated in the will?

### Retrieved Context
---
**[1] RA386-ART863**
Path: BOOK III - DIFFERENT MODES OF ACQUIRING OWNERSHIP > TITLE IV.—SUCCESSION > CH 2 - TESTAMENTARY SUCCESSION > SEC 3.—Substitution of Heirs > Art. 863
Text: A fideicommissary substitution by virtue of which the fiduciary or first heir instituted is entrusted with the obligation to preserve and to transmit to a second heir the whole or part of the inheritance, shall be valid and shall take effect, provided such substitution does not go beyond one degree from the heir originally instituted, and provided further, that the fiduciary or first heir and the second heir are living at the time of the death of the testator.
Source: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocsfriendly/2/53360
---

Under Article 863 of the Civil Code, a fideicommissary substitution is valid only if it does not go beyond one degree from the heir originally instituted, and both the fiduciary (first heir) and the second heir are living at the time of the testator's death. In your situation, the will creates a fideicommissary substitution: your brother is the fiduciary (first heir) obligated to preserve the land and transmit it to your son (second heir). Since both your brother and your son were alive at your father's death, that condition is satisfied. However, the substitution must not go beyond one degree from the original heir. This means there can be only one substitution after the original heir (your brother to your son), and no further substitutions. If the will also states that your son must later pass the land to his own son (your grandson), that would constitute a second degree substitution from the original heir, which exceeds the one-degree limit. Therefore, the further substitution in favor of your grandson would be void. The substitution in favor of your son remains valid, so your son will receive the property upon your brother's death, but he will not be legally obligated to pass it on to his own son. This assumes no other grounds of invalidity exist under the law.

Therefore, the oral sale is enforceable despite the lack of a written contract. The conduct of both parties—agreeing on the price, receiving payment, and delivering the item—supports the existence of a valid contract of sale under Article 1483.

Can you explain Article 459 of the Philippine Civil Code regarding land transferred by a river?

Article 459 of the Philippine Civil Code states that when a river, creek, or torrent carries away a known portion of land from one estate and deposits it on another estate, the owner of the land from which the portion was separated retains ownership of that portion, provided he removes it within two years. If he fails to remove it within that period, the owner of the land where it was deposited may acquire ownership. This rule applies to sudden transfers (avulsion) and is different from gradual deposits (alluvion).

Can you explain Article 1335 of the Philippine Civil Code?

Article 1335 of the Philippine Civil Code explains that violence and intimidation can make consent invalid. Violence is using serious or irresistible force to get someone's consent. A guardian sold a parcel of land belonging to a minor for ₱500,000. The actual market value of the land at the time of sale was ₱1,200,000. Path: BOOK IV - OBLIGATIONS AND CONTRACTS > TITLE II.—CONTRACTS > CH 6 - RESCISSIBLE CONTRACTS > Art. 1381
Text: The following contracts are rescissible:
(1) Those which are entered into by guardians whenever the wards whom they represent suffer lesion by more than one-fourth of the value of the things which are the object thereof;
(2) Those agreed upon in representation of absentees, if the latter suffer the lesion stated in the preceding number;
(3) Those undertaken in fraud of creditors when the latter cannot in any other manner collect the claims due them;
(4) Those which refer to things under litigation if they have been entered into by the defendant without the knowledge and approval of the litigants or of competent judicial authority;

Yes, the contract may be rescinded. Under Article 1381(1) of the Civil Code, a contract entered into by a guardian is rescissible if the ward suffers lesion by more than one-fourth of the value of the things which are the object thereof. In this case, the land was sold for ₱500,000 while its actual value was ₱1,200,000, resulting in a lesion of ₱700,000. This amount is more than one-fourth (25%) of ₱1,200,000, which is ₱300,000; thus, the requirement of lesion exceeding one-fourth is satisfied. The minor, or his legal representative, may file an action for rescission to set aside the sale and recover the property, subject to the rules on rescission under Articles 1380 to 1389. It is important to note that rescission is not automatic; it requires a judicial action and may be barred if the property has already passed to an innocent third party in good faith.

Article 941 covers legacies of generic personal property and devises of indeterminate real property. Under Article 419 of the Civil Code, property is either of public dominion or of private ownership. Public dominion property is owned by the State or its political subdivisions and is intended for public use, public service, or the development of national wealth. Private ownership property is owned by private individuals or entities. In your situation, the determination of whether the vacant lot is public dominion or private depends on who owns it and its purpose. If the lot is actually owned by the barangay (a local government unit) and is being used as a basketball court for public recreation, it would be classified as public dominion property because it is owned by a public entity and intended for public use. Can you explain Article 1544 of the Philippine Civil Code about double sale?

Article 1544 deals with what happens when the same property is sold to two different buyers. If the property is movable (like a car or furniture), the ownership goes to the buyer who first takes possession of it in good faith (meaning they did not know about the other sale). If the property is immovable (like land or a house), the ownership goes to the buyer who first records the sale in the Registry of Property, provided they are in good faith. If no one has registered, then the first buyer to take possession in good faith gets ownership. If neither has registered nor taken possession, then the buyer with the oldest title (the earliest sale document) who is in good faith will own the property.

Article 2078 provides that if a creditor releases one guarantor from his obligation without the consent of the other guarantors, that release benefits all guarantors to the extent of the share of the released guarantor. I was supposed to deliver my specific vintage car (a 1965 Mustang) to a buyer as part of a sale. Before the delivery date and without any fault on my part, a typhoon caused a tree to fall on the car, totally destroying it. I had not yet incurred delay. Path: BOOK IV - OBLIGATIONS AND CONTRACTS > TITLE I.—OBLIGATIONS > CH 4 - EXTINGUISHMENT OF OBLIGATIONS > SEC 2.—Loss of the Thing Due > Art. 1262
Text: An obligation which consists in the delivery of a determinate thing shall be extinguished if it should be lost or destroyed without the fault of the debtor, and before he has incurred in delay.
When by law or stipulation, the obligor is liable even for fortuitous events, the loss of the thing does not extinguish the obligation, and he shall be responsible for damages. The same rule applies when the nature of the obligation requires the assumption of risk.
Source: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocsfriendly/2/53360
---

Under Article 1262, your obligation to deliver the determinate thing (the specific car) is extinguished because the thing was lost or destroyed without your fault and before you incurred delay. The typhoon is a fortuitous event. However, if there was a stipulation in your contract that you would be liable even for fortuitous events, or if the nature of the obligation (e.g., an obligation to deliver at your own risk) requires assumption of risk, then the obligation is not extinguished and you would be liable for damages. In your case, unless such stipulation or risk assumption exists, you are not liable and the buyer cannot demand delivery or damages.

### Question
My aunt passed away and in her will, she left a house and lot to my husband and me, stating that 70% should go to me and 30% to my husband. We are under the conjugal partnership of gains. Will this property become part of our conjugal property? Or is it separate for each of us?

Path: BOOK I - PERSONS > TITLE VI.—PROPERTY RELATIONS BETWEEN - HUSBAND AND WIFE > CH 4 - CONJUGAL PARTNERSHIP OF GAINS > SEC 2.—Exclusive Property of Each Spouse > Art. 150
Text: Property donated or left by will to the spouses, jointly and with designation of determinate shares, shall pertain to the wife as paraphernal property, and to the husband as capital, in the proportion specified by the donor or testator, and in the absence of designation, share and share alike, without prejudice to what is provided in article 753.

Under Article 150 of the Civil Code, when property is left by will to spouses jointly with designated shares, the property does not become conjugal. Instead, each spouse owns their designated share as exclusive property. In your case, the 70% share left to you is your paraphernal property (exclusive to you), and the 30% share left to your husband is his capital (exclusive to him). These shares are not part of the conjugal partnership of gains. If your aunt had not specified any shares, you and your husband would have owned the property equally, share and share alike. This rule is without prejudice to Article 753, which may impose certain general rules on donations to multiple persons.

Under Article 1393 of the Civil Code, ratification may be express or tacit. Tacit ratification is understood if, with knowledge of the reason which renders the contract voidable and such reason having ceased, the person who has a right to invoke it should execute an act which necessarily implies an intention to waive his right. Ibig sabihin, hindi mo siya maaaring piliting bilhin ang lupa sa pamamagitan ng kaso sa hukuman dahil hindi tatanggapin ng hukom ang ebidensyang pawang salitaan lamang ukol sa bentahan ng lupa.
